analysis.one_liner: Bans organophosphates, neonicotinoids, and paraquat and strengthens pesticide safety rules.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Agriculture Committee; it received no hearing, no vote, and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would overhaul the main federal pesticide law. It would immediately ban three classes of pesticides linked to harm in children and wildlife, automatically suspend any pesticide the European Union or Canada has banned, require full disclosure of hidden 'inert' ingredients, stop the sale of banned pesticide stockpiles, let local communities set stricter rules, and create new safety protections for farmworkers, including mandatory reporting of poisonings and protection from retaliation. It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and never received any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Farmworkers, children, rural residents, and consumers exposed to pesticide residues, plus pollinators and endangered wildlife that current pesticides harm.

how_it_helps.text: Immediately cancels registration of organophosphates, neonicotinoids, and paraquat and bans their sale, use, and future registration, citing links to neurodevelopmental damage in children, Parkinson's disease, and pollinator decline.
Requires the EPA to suspend any pesticide banned by the European Union or Canada, noting the U.S. allows 72 pesticides the EU has banned or is phasing out.
Requires pesticide labels to list all inert ingredients, which can make up 99 percent of a product and may include carcinogens.

Creates mandatory reporting of farmworker pesticide poisonings, fines employers who fail to report, offers $25,000 rewards for reporting, protects farmworkers from retaliation, and shields them from immigration action based on a report.
Lets local communities enact stricter pesticide protections than their states allow and lets any person sue the EPA for failing to comply with the pesticide law.

analysis.who_pays: Pesticide manufacturers that make paraquat, organophosphates, and neonicotinoids would lose registered products, and farmers who rely on them would need alternatives.

drawbacks.text: The bill cancels whole classes of pesticides by operation of law without the EPA's normal scientific review or any economic analysis, and it expressly prohibits the agency from weighing the costs and benefits of continuing a pesticide when reviewing bans from other countries.

Automatic suspension based on EU or Canada decisions effectively outsources U.S. pesticide safety determinations to foreign regulators, which critics would call a loss of independent scientific judgment.
Immediate bans without transition could leave some growers without practical alternatives for certain pests in a planting season, with costs passed to food prices.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real, documented gap: farmworkers are disproportionately poisoned by pesticides with weak reporting and retaliation protections, and the U.S. still allows dozens of pesticides banned abroad. The costs fall on a concentrated industry and some growers, but the abrupt, no-exceptions ban mechanism and refusal to weigh economic effects are blunt and could have been designed with transitions.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and then to a subcommittee, and it never received a markup or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. James McGovern introduced the bill on July 28, 2023 with 13 original cosponsors, all Democrats.
It was referred to the House Committee on Agriculture and then to the Subcommittee on Conservation, Research, and Biotechnology on September 26, 2023.
The House Agriculture Committee never scheduled the bill for a markup or hearing, and no version was introduced in the Senate, so it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pesticide manufacturers, including makers of paraquat and neonicotinoids, kept their registered products on the market, and farmworkers and consumers gained no new protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pesticide manufacturers kept their products on sale

for.name: Rep. James P. McGovern
for.role: Sponsor, House Democratic chief deputy whip-style senior member from Massachusetts
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 13 original cosponsors.

for.name: 22 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Khanna, Grijalva, Raskin, Nadler, and Lynch.

against.name: House Committee on Agriculture (Chair Glenn Thompson)
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee and never scheduled it for a hearing or markup, so it never reached the House floor.

against.name: Pesticide industry
against.role: Manufacturers of paraquat, organophosphates, and neonicotinoids
against.what_they_did: The bill would ban their flagship products and eliminate their registered markets; the industry historically defends the pesticide law's review process.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 22 cosponsors were Democrats, and the Republican-led Agriculture Committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill immediately cancels registrations for paraquat, organophosphates, and neonicotinoids and bans sales of existing stock, wiping out registered markets for products central to these companies' sales. Its death leaves those markets intact.
Growers rely on the banned insecticides for pest control and would have faced adaptation costs, though the bill also removes pesticide exposure risks their workers face.
Banning neonicotinoids and organophosphates reduces contamination of neighboring fields and pollinator decline, advantages producers selling on reduced-pesticide claims.
